name: Longest tape with even vowel counts
brief:
A machine writes one lowercase letter per event to the string `tape`. Return the length of the longest stretch of consecutive letters in which each of `a`, `e`, `i`, `o` and `u` appears an even number of times. Zero times is even.

Write `longest_even_vowels(tape)`.

Example. In `"xaeyea"` the whole tape holds `a` twice and `e` twice, so the answer is 6.
constraints: $O(n)$ time is the target. Counting the vowels of every stretch is too slow.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Keep five bits, one per vowel, flipped each time that vowel appears. A stretch is even exactly when the bits before it and at its end are equal, so store the first position of each bit pattern.

examples.note: The whole tape holds two of a and two of e, so all 6 letters count.
Every stretch holds some vowel once, so no stretch is even.

tests.call: longest_even_vowels("".join("aeioubcd"[(i * i + 3 * i) % 8] for i in range(200000)))

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The large tests need the step from counting vowels in every stretch to a dict of the first position of each parity pattern.
notes: Five parity bits summarise the vowels so far, and equal patterns bound an even stretch.
The empty prefix has pattern 0 at position -1, and only the first position of a pattern is kept.
One pass with at most 32 patterns in the dict, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: It never records pattern 0 before the tape starts, so a stretch from the first letter is missed.
It overwrites each pattern with its latest position, so it measures from the nearest match, not the earliest.
It tries the longest stretches first and counts each afresh, which is far too slow on a long tape.
